basis: New mission, no workbook source; authored per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. Facts and sources: NHI single-payer system began 1995, near-universal coverage, run by 衛福部中央健康保險署 (NHI Administration). Premium rate held at 5.17% since 2021, confirmed unchanged for 2025 and 2026 by the NHI committee (全民健康保險會, Nov 2024 meeting; UHO/HakkaNews Nov 2025 coverage), vs South Korea ~7% and Japan ~10%. Safety reserve (安全準備金) projected at ~2.1-2.2 months of benefit payments at end of 2025 per the Nov 2024 committee meeting (mohw.gov.tw cp-4624 series; wantrich.chinatimes.com 2026-05-09 coverage of Minister 石崇良). Taiwan crossed 20% 65+ population in 2025 (467.3万, 20.06%), officially a "super-aged society" per Ministry of Interior data (CNA 2026-01-09 reports; 14% threshold reached 2018). Old-age dependency ratio ~27 per 100 working-age residents in 2025 (moi.gov.tw statistical bulletin); longer-range ~2 working-age adults per elderly by 2040 cited via globaltaiwan.org/Brookings commentary — kept general, not stated as a precise official figure. National medical-expenditure long-range projection (~NT$1.3 trillion circa 2020 rising several-fold by mid-century) from a government science-policy forecast (cited via ctee.com.tw), kept in general terms per playbook guidance since the multiple is approximate. Health spending ~6.6-6.9% of GDP vs OECD ~9.7%, Japan ~10.6%, South Korea ~8.4%, US ~17% (mohw.gov.tw national health expenditure report; twreporter.org OECD comparison piece). NHI total annual budget passed NT$800 billion circa 2022 (mohw.gov.tw cp-5020-63299). Health Bank (健康存摺) ~12 million users, several hundred million data views, now linking Google/Apple/Garmin wearable data via SDK (mohw.gov.tw cp-16-79026 Google/NHI Administration release). "AI-on-DM" partnership with Google and National Health Research Institutes announced 2024 to predict type-2 diabetes complications, planned to extend to other chronic diseases (blog.google zh-tw 2024 Cloud Summit Taipei release; taiwan-healthcare.org coverage; cohesiondata.com news). Family-medicine/大家醫計畫 integrated-care clinics described only in general terms ("thousands of clinics") since an exact current count was not confirmed. No partisan cross-strait framing used. Register and structure per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md; calibration matched to content/authored/levels/sdg13-1.*.json.

slides.1: An NHI card sits in nearly every wallet on this island, yet few of us ever interrogate what keeps the system financially solvent behind it. Long-term sustainability, not present-day access, is now the genuinely open question.
slides.2: SDG 3 establishes a single global objective, covering mental wellbeing alongside physical health, and Taiwan has pursued something like it for three decades already. The system simply lacked that particular name until recently.
slides.3: Run as a single, unified plan since 1995, Taiwan's National Health Insurance now covers nearly the entire resident population. That is precisely why health economists abroad keep studying it as a model system.
slides.4: By 2025, Taiwan had formally entered super-aged territory, with more than a fifth of residents aged 65 or above. Only seven years earlier that fraction sat at a mere 14 percent, and the upward trajectory continues.
slides.5: As the population ages, national medical spending is projected to expand many times over in the coming decades. That growth is driven less by any single crisis than by the accumulated needs of older patients.
slides.6: What should concern you is this: the premium rate has remained frozen since 2021, even as expenditures keep climbing around it. Meanwhile, the safety reserve underpinning the entire system has been quietly contracting, year after year.
slides.7: Nearly universal since it launched in 1995, NHI has sustained that coverage for three decades now. Few developed health systems, including some far wealthier ones, have matched this level of near-universal reach.
slides.8: Health care in Taiwan consumes a markedly smaller slice of GDP than in Japan, South Korea or the United States. Out-of-pocket costs here remain consistently low while coverage stays comprehensive, a combination few health systems accomplish simultaneously.
slides.9: The NHI Administration has built a digital Health Bank, used by millions of citizens, that now accepts data sent from wearable apps. Personal physical data now sits alongside official medical records for the first time.
slides.10: Policymakers face a genuine trade-off between two blunt instruments: raising the premium rate outright, or widening the income base it draws from. Neither option leaves everyone equally satisfied, no matter which one is chosen.
slides.11: One credible fix lies considerably upstream of the hospital. Family doctors, tracking patients over multiple years instead of treating sudden crises, can catch illness while it still remains cheap to manage.
slides.12: Piloted with partners including Google, AI models now scan shared medical records to flag long-term disease risk years in advance. The system's posture is shifting from late treatment toward genuine early intervention.
slides.13: Should the safety reserve keep contracting, it will eventually breach the floor regulators require it to hold. At that point, the government would be forced into rapid, less considered action.
slides.14: Even if premiums do rise, that additional burden will not be distributed evenly across the population. It is young workers and recent graduates, already earning comparatively little, who would absorb a higher rate most severely.
slides.15: Some insist Taiwan should simply match Japan's or South Korea's higher premium rate. Yet a larger estimate alone does not explain why expenditures keep climbing, nor does it restructure how care is actually administered.
slides.16: Time is not neutral in this story, either. Large cohorts of workers are retiring right now, shrinking the contributing population at precisely the moment the reserve can least afford it.
slides.17: So where does that leave the system? A substantial achievement, sitting under genuine structural strain, and it is the strain, not the achievement, that has intensified with every passing year.
slides.18: None of this is a distant, hypothetical debate. It is the premium you will eventually pay, and the care your own family will eventually require, regardless of whether you have seriously paused to consider it.
slides.19: STEM students bring something specific to this problem. They can read data honestly, build models that predict risk rather than merely describe it, and argue for trade-offs precisely rather than emotionally.
slides.20: Taiwan has built something genuinely rare here: substantial coverage at a price few comparable economies can match. What happens over the next three decades begins with what we, not someone else, choose to do today.
